Please confirm the following six items:

1. Site list conflict
The Demand Analysis report and the Business Case present two different 12-site networks. The Demand Analysis includes Cedarwick-Halston, Fairhaven-Rosmere, Alderby, and Kestrel Bay, whereas the Business Case includes Copper Glen, Ravensfield-Aurora Plant, and Juniper Wells instead. 2. Opex figure conflict
For the 12-site network, the original brief gives steady-state operating costs of CAD 48-64M/year, while Appendix 1 of the Business Case reports annual O&M of only CAD 4.2-5.6M/year. That is a roughly 11x difference. Which figure, or underlying cost basis, should drive the financial model's operating-cost assumption?

3. Availability payment sizing target
Should the availability payment be calculated only to meet the target minimum DSCR of 1.65x, or must it also achieve a minimum equity IRR within the 16-24% infrastructure-equity target range cited by the Business Case? Although the current DSCR-only approach reaches the coverage target, equity IRR remains negative even after the availability payment is added.

4. Programwide/shared costs
In addition to $201.5M of site-level capex, the Business Case's $234M Reference Case contains $18.4M for shared programwide costs, including the digital platform and program management, plus a $14M reserve/13th-site allowance. Should the model show these as separate line items, or should they remain outside the scope of the 12-site financial model?

5. Financing terms confirmation
Senior debt in the Business Case covers 45-60% of capital, is priced at 425-575bps above Government of Canada bond yields, and may be supplemented by optional mezzanine debt. Our current model instead uses a simplified 55/45 debt/equity split with a flat 9% rate. At this stage, is that single-tranche structure acceptable, or should mezzanine financing be modeled separately?

6. Tax/depreciation
At present, the model applies a flat 34% tax to EBITDA and includes no depreciation shield. Is that sufficient for this stage, or should depreciation/CCA (Capital Cost Allowance) be incorporated because this will be an actual government submission?

source_message.speaker: freelancer
source_message.text:
Hi Mari,

Sure I will make the required changes. The model looks detailed because it's built on individual drivers each revenue stream (parking, pods, fleet, digital, ancillary) and each cost line is calculated separately from its own assumption, rather than typed in as one lump number. I did it this way on purpose so that when the government reviewer asks "where does this figure come from?", every number traces back to a source on the Assumptions tab. That's what makes it defensible.

The trade-off is exactly what you're feeling , more drivers , more rows to look at. I can go either way, so I'd rather you decide:

(a) Keep it driver-based (defensible, more rows), or
(b) Collapse it to a summary model a handful of top-level lines (total revenue, total cost, debt, availability payment, returns) with the detailed build moved to hidden/backing tabs. The front page becomes very short and clean; the detail is still there if anyone wants to open it.

I can make it a one-pager but still has the audit trail underneath. Tell me which you'd prefer and I'll restructure accordingly.

A few structuring options came up that could genuinely strengthen your pitch to government. These aren't in the model yet; I'm flagging them because any one of them could be the thing that makes the submission stand out. Such as:

1\. Government-funds-first, then sublet against the income ("build-then-transfer"). The Province funds or co-funds the capex up front (cheapest capital in the room), then leases/sublets the operating network to a private operator who pays a concession fee back against parking, pod and fleet income. This flips the story instead of government paying an availability payment out, government recovers a return in. I can model this as a third case (Case H) it may show a far lower net cost to the Province than the availability-payment route.

2\. Availability payment now, tapering to a revenue-share later. Rather than a flat 24-year payment, structure it so the Province pays more in the early ramp-up years (when revenue is thin) and then, once the network matures and throws off surplus cash, the Province shares in the upside clawing back part of what it paid in. Same bankability, lower lifetime net cost, and it reads as a partnership rather than a subsidy.

3\. Toll / user-levy overlay on the corridor. If these sites sit on designated freight corridors, a small per-truck corridor levy (or a portion of an existing road-use charge) could be ring-fenced to part-fund the network. That directly reduces the availability payment the government has to find from general revenue the users who benefit help pay.

4\. Phased equity exit / refinancing at stabilisation. Model the Province (or the original equity) selling down its stake to a pension fund or infrastructure fund once the network is built and de-risked (around year 9-12). De-risked, cash-yielding infrastructure sells at a premium so early capital gets recycled out at a profit and redeployed into Phase 4, instead of being locked up for 24 years.

5\. Anchor / cornerstone tenant revenue. Lock in four or five large fleets or a fuel/EV/retail partner on a long-term take-or-pay contract at the flagship hubs before financial close. Even a modest guaranteed floor on revenue materially improves the DSCR and can shrink the availability payment lenders require it's the single fastest way to make the numbers look stronger without changing the build.

Happy to build any of these into the model as additional cases options 1 and 2 in particular could meaningfully cut the headline cost to government, which is exactly what makes a submission persuasive. Let me know which direction you'd like, and whether to go simple (b) or keep it detailed, and I'll turn it around.

Best,
Elias

Hi Mari,

Sure I will make the required changes. The model looks detailed because it's built on individual drivers each revenue stream (parking, pods, fleet, digital, ancillary) and each cost line is calculated separately from its own assumption, rather than typed in as one lump number. I did it this way on purpose so that when the government reviewer asks "where does this figure come from?", every number traces back to a source on the Assumptions tab. That's what makes it defensible.

The trade-off is exactly what you're feeling , more drivers , more rows to look at. I can go either way, so I'd rather you decide:

(a) Keep it driver-based (defensible, more rows), or
(b) Collapse it to a summary model a handful of top-level lines (total revenue, total cost, debt, availability payment, returns) with the detailed build moved to hidden/backing tabs. The front page becomes very short and clean; the detail is still there if anyone wants to open it.

I can make it a one-pager but still has the audit trail underneath. Tell me which you'd prefer and I'll restructure accordingly.

A few structuring options came up that could genuinely strengthen your pitch to government. These aren't in the model yet; I'm flagging them because any one of them could be the thing that makes the submission stand out. Such as:

1\. Government-funds-first, then sublet against the income ("build-then-transfer"). The Province funds or co-funds the capex up front (cheapest capital in the room), then leases/sublets the operating network to a private operator who pays a concession fee back against parking, pod and fleet income. This flips the story instead of government paying an availability payment out, government recovers a return in. I can model this as a third case (Case H) it may show a far lower net cost to the Province than the availability-payment route.

2\. Availability payment now, tapering to a revenue-share later. Rather than a flat 24-year payment, structure it so the Province pays more in the early ramp-up years (when revenue is thin) and then, once the network matures and throws off surplus cash, the Province shares in the upside clawing back part of what it paid in. Same bankability, lower lifetime net cost, and it reads as a partnership rather than a subsidy.

3\. Toll / user-levy overlay on the corridor. If these sites sit on designated freight corridors, a small per-truck corridor levy (or a portion of an existing road-use charge) could be ring-fenced to part-fund the network. That directly reduces the availability payment the government has to find from general revenue the users who benefit help pay.

4\. Phased equity exit / refinancing at stabilisation. Model the Province (or the original equity) selling down its stake to a pension fund or infrastructure fund once the network is built and de-risked (around year 9-12). De-risked, cash-yielding infrastructure sells at a premium so early capital gets recycled out at a profit and redeployed into Phase 4, instead of being locked up for 24 years.

5\. Anchor / cornerstone tenant revenue. Lock in four or five large fleets or a fuel/EV/retail partner on a long-term take-or-pay contract at the flagship hubs before financial close. Even a modest guaranteed floor on revenue materially improves the DSCR and can shrink the availability payment lenders require it's the single fastest way to make the numbers look stronger without changing the build.

Happy to build any of these into the model as additional cases options 1 and 2 in particular could meaningfully cut the headline cost to government, which is exactly what makes a submission persuasive. Let me know which direction you'd like, and whether to go simple (b) or keep it detailed, and I'll turn it around.

Best,
Elias

source_message.text: As I said earlier, requesting accountability for the delivered work is not exploitative, so that accusation does not make sense. source_message.speaker: freelancer
source_message.text:
Ending the contract here is fine with me, and I would like both sides to handle that professionally.

For the record, the first draft was delivered on time and addressed everything in the original brief. After you said it was difficult to follow, I responded directly rather than ignoring that feedback by producing a second, extensively reworked version. It included a simplified dashboard, clearly sourced assumptions, separate cash flows for both funding scenarios, additional financial statements and a short summary presentation to make the review easier. The second deliverable was sent before your refund request. Despite my asking, I received no specific review comments on that version or on the first draft.

Since both milestones were completed and delivered according to scope, I will not issue a refund. Instead, I’ll use Upwork’s dispute process to pursue resolution of the remaining milestone payment. You may leave whichever review you believe is accurate, and I will do the same; the delivered work and our message history can speak for themselves.

execution.observed_behavior: The freelancer reports producing and delivering a substantially reworked second version in response to the difficult-to-follow feedback, with changes intended to make review easier.

source_message.speaker: client
source_message.text:
Reviewing and following the current model is difficult because it is too complex. Its dashboards also fail to show decision-makers the essential information clearly, including project returns, debt performance, and overall bankability. The revised model should therefore be simpler, easier to understand, and easier to audit, with stronger dashboards and project-finance analysis. My goal is a model that works technically while also making a clear case that the project is financially viable, bankable, and attractive to investors.
